headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Isolation in Healthcare
headings.content: Isolation in healthcare refers to the practice of separating patients who have communicable diseases from other patients, visitors, and healthcare staff. This measure stops the spread of infectious agents within healthcare settings. Isolation serves as a crucial line of defense in Nigerian hospitals where infectious diseases like Lassa fever, tuberculosis, and cholera remain prevalent. Understanding this concept protects both the community and the clinical team.

headings.title: Chain of Infection and Rationale for Isolation Precautions
headings.content: The chain of infection consists of six links: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, and susceptible host. Isolation precautions interrupt this chain primarily by blocking the mode of transmission. For example, placing a patient with open wound infections in contact isolation stops the pathogen from moving via hands or equipment to another patient.

headings.title: Standard Precautions: The Foundation of Patient Care
headings.content:
Standard precautions apply to all patients receiving care in any healthcare setting, regardless of their diagnosed or suspected infection status. These measures assume that every body fluid, non-intact skin, and mucous membrane may contain transmissible infectious agents.

- **Hand hygiene**: Washing with soap and water or using alcohol-based rub before and after contact.
- **Personal protective equipment**: Wearing gloves, gowns, masks, and eye protection when splashes are likely.
- **Respiratory hygiene**: Covering coughs and sneezes with tissues or the inner elbow.
- **Safe injection practices**: Using sterile syringes and needles once without recapping.

headings.title: Transmission-Based Precautions: Airborne, Droplet, and Contact
headings.content:
When standard precautions are insufficient, transmission-based precautions are added based on how the pathogen spreads.

- **Airborne precautions**: Used for pathogens spread via small droplet nuclei remaining in the air over time, such as tuberculosis. Requires negative pressure rooms and N95 respirators.
- **Droplet precautions**: Used for pathogens spread through close respiratory droplets, such as influenza. Requires surgical masks within one meter of the patient.
- **Contact precautions**: Used for pathogens spread by direct or indirect touch, such as multi-resistant organisms. Requires gowns and gloves upon entry.

headings.title: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE): Donning and Doffing Protocols
headings.content:
Putting on (donning) and taking off (doffing) PPE safely prevents self-contamination. Errors during removal often lead to accidental exposure.

| Action | Correct Sequence | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Donning | Gown, Mask, Goggles, Gloves | Protects skin and clothing first, hands last |
| Doffing | Gloves, Goggles, Gown, Mask | Removes dirtiest items first, clean mask last |

headings.title: Management of the Isolated Patient: Environment and Logistics
headings.content: Managing an isolated patient involves controlling the physical environment and managing hospital logistics. Dedicated medical equipment such as stethoscopes and blood pressure cuffs must stay in the room to prevent cross-contamination. Waste and linen handling require biohazard labeling and leak-proof bags. Limiting room entry by consolidating nursing tasks reduces supply consumption and staff exposure.

headings.title: Psychosocial Impact of Isolation on Patients and Families
headings.content: Isolation precautions often cause feelings of loneliness, anxiety, and depression due to sensory deprivation and limited human contact. Patients may feel stigmatized, believing staff fear them. Nurses mitigate these effects by scheduling regular interaction, offering communication devices like phones, and explaining the clinical necessity of the precautions clearly.

headings.title: Infection Control and Nursing Responsibilities
headings.content: Nurses play a central role in maintaining infection control standards across the health facility. Responsibilities include auditing compliance with hand hygiene, educating patients and visitors on barrier methods, and promptly reporting communicable disease outbreaks to hospital epidemiologists. Diligent documentation ensures continuity of care and supports institutional surveillance efforts.
